title: He Left Hyderabad With $8. His Company Just Put $1 Billion Back Into India — and Wants to Buy a Whole Bank.
excerpt: Prem Watsa's Fairfax snapped up nearly a billion dollars of Indian government bonds in a single day. The real target is IDBI Bank, in what could be India's biggest bank privatisation ever.
body:
Prem Watsa left Hyderabad for Canada with eight dollars in his pocket. Decades later, his company just quietly parked nearly a billion of them back into Indian government paper — and the move may be the opening gambit in what could become the single largest foreign acquisition of an Indian bank.

Fairfax India Holding Corp, the Indian investment arm of Watsa's Toronto-based Fairfax Financial Holdings, bought approximately $1 billion of Indian government bonds in a single session last Friday, according to five sources who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity. The scale is extraordinary: at the end of December 2025, Fairfax India's entire government securities portfolio was worth just $42.6 million. The purchase was roughly 23 times that.

Why Bonds, Why Now

The answer is IDBI Bank.

The Indian government and Life Insurance Corporation of India together hold 94.7 per cent of the state-owned lender — 45.48 per cent and 49.24 per cent respectively — and have been trying to sell a combined 60.7 per cent stake since 2022 as part of a broader privatisation programme. Fairfax, alongside Emirates NBD and Kotak Mahindra Bank, was among the shortlisted bidders. But the process stalled in March when all bids came in below the government's reserve price.

Now talks have revived. Fairfax has submitted a revised bid and proposed to make IDBI Bank its anchor investment in India's financial services sector, according to a Moneycontrol report. The all-cash deal is expected to fetch approximately ₹50,000 crore — just over $5 billion — for the government and LIC combined, with Fairfax quoting around ₹77 per share. The divestment could close by September.

The billion-dollar bond purchase served a dual purpose. India recently exempted foreign investors in government bonds from capital gains tax, making the transaction commercially viable. More importantly, it moved capital into the country ahead of a potential deal — capital that would be readily available for the IDBI acquisition without the delays of a cross-border transfer.

> ""Fairfax is not a regular participant in the Indian bond markets," one treasury official noted."

The Bonds Tell a Story

Treasury officials told Reuters that the buying was concentrated at the short end: approximately ₹60 billion ($633.7 million) of the 6.03 per cent bond maturing in 2029, bought at a yield five basis points below prevailing market levels. Fairfax also likely acquired ₹6 billion of the 6.79 per cent 2027 bond and ₹26 billion in Treasury bills maturing in May and June 2027.

Short-duration paper is precisely what you buy when you expect to need the money within two to three years — the timeline for closing, funding, and stabilising a major bank acquisition. "Fairfax is not a regular participant in the Indian bond markets," one treasury official noted. The sheer unusualness of the trade is part of its signal value.

A Diaspora Homecoming

Watsa's story reads like a screenplay commissioned by Indiaspora. Born in 1950, he attended Hyderabad Public School and the Indian Institute of Technology Madras before emigrating to Canada, where he sold furnaces and air conditioners to put himself through an MBA at the University of Western Ontario.

In 1985, he took over Markel Financial, a small Canadian trucking insurance company teetering on the edge of bankruptcy, renamed it Fairfax Financial Holdings, and built it into a firm with annual revenues exceeding $8 billion and a market capitalisation of roughly C$37 billion. The financial press dubbed him "the Canadian Warren Buffett."

If the IDBI deal closes, it would be among the largest foreign direct investments in an Indian financial institution — a Hyderabad-born IIT graduate returning capital to the country he left with almost nothing. Watsa's son Benjamin took over as Fairfax India's chairman on July 1, marking a generational transition within the company even as its biggest Indian bet takes shape.

What IDBI Gets — and What Fairfax Gives Up

IDBI Bank is not a trophy asset in the conventional sense. In 2018, nearly a third of its loan book was classified as bad. The crisis eroded its capital base and forced the government to press LIC into pumping in ₹21,600 crore to raise its stake from 8 per cent to 51 per cent. Years of cleanup have improved the balance sheet, but the bank's shares still trade below where they were 13 years ago.

What attracts Fairfax is the platform: a nationwide branch network, a banking licence that is almost impossible to obtain in India, and the operational leverage that comes with privatisation — shedding government bureaucracy, rationalising staff costs, and making lending decisions on commercial merit.

Fairfax has committed that IDBI Bank will be its sole banking investment. That means divesting its existing 40 per cent stake in CSB Bank, the former Catholic Syrian Bank that Fairfax rescued in 2018. RBI regulations prohibit a single promoter from holding two banking licences, and Fairfax has signalled it is willing to exit CSB entirely to make the IDBI acquisition work.

The Bigger Picture

The IDBI sale is the centrepiece of India's disinvestment agenda. The Centre's asset monetisation target for 2025–26 stands at ₹47,000 crore, and IDBI is expected to be the single largest contributor. A successful privatisation would also send a signal to global markets that India can complete a large, complex divestment — something critics have questioned after years of delays.

For the diaspora, Watsa's billion-dollar bond play is a reminder that the relationship between India and its overseas community is no longer just about remittances and nostalgia. It is about capital, control, and the institutional confidence to bet big on a country that some of its most successful children left decades ago — and are now, in a sense, coming back to.
